quests.instruction: Which gives Earth its daytime light?
quests.hint: Consider the star that shines on us.
quests.explanation: The Sun is a star that sends light and warmth to Earth, giving us day on the side facing it.
quests.funFact: The Sun's light takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.

quests.instruction: When it is day on one side of Earth, what is it on the opposite side?
quests.hint: Earth is a ball, and the Sun can only light one half.
quests.explanation: The Sun lights only half of Earth at a time, so the other half is in the dark.
quests.funFact: At any moment, half of Earth is having day.

quests.instruction: What spins to give us day and night?
quests.hint: One of these turns around once a day.
quests.explanation: Earth spins like a top, so places turn toward and away from the Sun.
quests.funFact: Earth spins once about every twenty-four hours.

quests.instruction: Why does the Sun appear to move across the sky?
options: Because the Sun is traveling around us
quests.hint: Picture riding in a car and watching trees.
quests.explanation: The Sun seems to move because Earth spins, like trees seem to move when we ride past them.
quests.funFact: The Sun stays near the center of our solar system.

quests.instruction: A lamp shines on a ball in a dark room. Which part of the ball is bright?
quests.hint: Imagine Earth as a ball and the Sun as the lamp.
quests.explanation: The side facing the light is lit, like Earth's daytime side.
quests.funFact: Scientists often use a globe and a lamp to model day and night.

quests.instruction: If you are standing on the side of Earth turned away from the Sun, it is...
quests.explanation: The side of Earth facing away from the Sun is dark, so it is night there.
quests.funFact: The dark side of Earth is not completely dark. Moonlight, stars, and city lights still shine.

quests.instruction: How long does it take for Earth to spin around once?
quests.hint: One full spin makes one day and night.
quests.explanation: Earth spins once in about twenty-four hours, which gives us a day.
quests.funFact: One trip around the Sun takes about a year.

quests.instruction: What happens when your part of Earth turns toward the Sun?
quests.explanation: When Earth turns toward the Sun, we see sunrise.
quests.funFact: Sunrise sweeps around the world as Earth turns, reaching different places one after another.

quests.instruction: When it is afternoon where you live, what might it be on the other side of Earth?
quests.explanation: The opposite side of Earth is turned away from the Sun, so it is night.
quests.funFact: Earth is divided into about twenty-four main time zones, roughly one for each hour of the day.

quests.instruction: Which one is true?
quests.correctAnswer: Earth spins, so the Sun seems to move
options: The Sun circles Earth every single day
Earth spins, so the Sun seems to move
quests.explanation: Earth spins, which makes the Sun, Moon, and stars seem to travel across the sky.
quests.funFact: People once thought the Sun circled Earth.

quests.instruction: Why is it dark at night?
quests.correctAnswer: Our side faces away from the Sun
options: Our side faces away from the Sun
quests.explanation: Night comes when our side of Earth has turned to face away from the Sun.
quests.funFact: Even at night, the Sun is still shining on the other half of Earth.

quests.instruction: What does Earth's spinning cause?
quests.explanation: Spinning gives day and night, while the tilt and trip around the Sun give seasons.
quests.funFact: Because of Earth's spin, a point on the equator moves at more than 1,600 kilometers per hour.

quests.instruction: Who is correct? "The Moon makes its own light" or "The Moon reflects sunlight"?
options: The Moon makes its own light
quests.explanation: The Moon shines because it reflects sunlight.
quests.funFact: The Moon changes shape in the sky, called phases, because we see different amounts of its sunlit half.

quests.instruction: If Earth stopped spinning, what would happen to the side facing the Sun?
options: It would turn to night quickly
quests.hint: Remember the side facing the Sun.
quests.explanation: If Earth stopped spinning, one side would stay in light and the other in dark.
quests.funFact: Earth has been spinning for billions of years.

quests.instruction: Which direction does the Sun seem to rise?
quests.explanation: The Sun appears to rise in the east because Earth spins toward the east.
quests.funFact: For most places on Earth, the Sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west.

quests.instruction: What is the Sun?
quests.explanation: The Sun is a star, a huge ball of hot, glowing gas.
quests.funFact: The Sun is the nearest star to Earth.

quests.instruction: Which would be a good model for day and night?
quests.correctAnswer: A flashlight and a spinning ball
options: A flashlight and a flat paper
A flashlight and a spinning ball
quests.hint: Earth is a round ball that turns.
quests.explanation: A ball turning in front of a light shows how places go from light to dark.
quests.funFact: The oldest globe that still exists was made more than 500 years ago.

quests.instruction: When the Sun sets for you, what is happening to your part of Earth?
quests.correctAnswer: It is turning away from the Sun
options: It is turning away from the Sun
It is moving closer to the Sun
quests.explanation: Your place is turning away from the Sun as Earth spins.
quests.funFact: Sunset happens first in the east and later in places farther west.

quests.instruction: Which is true about the length of a day on Earth?
quests.hint: Consider how long it takes Earth to spin.
quests.explanation: A day is about 24 hours.
quests.funFact: A day on Mars is a little longer than a day on Earth, about twenty-four hours and forty minutes.

quests.instruction: A globe has a lamp shining on it. What would be dark?
quests.correctAnswer: The side away from the lamp
options: The side away from the lamp
quests.explanation: The side away from the light is dark, like Earth's night side.
quests.funFact: A globe is a model of Earth.

quests.instruction: What causes sunrise?
quests.explanation: As Earth spins, our place turns toward the Sun, and light appears.
quests.funFact: Earth's spin has been giving us sunrises for billions of years.

quests.instruction: At sunset it looks like the Sun goes down. What is really happening?
quests.correctAnswer: Our side of Earth is turning away
options: Our side of Earth is turning away
The Sun is falling out of the sky
quests.explanation: The Sun does not fall. Our part of Earth turns away from it, so the Sun seems to sink.
quests.funFact: The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth.

quests.instruction: Both day and night repeat because...
options: The Sun keeps moving away and back
quests.explanation: Earth's steady turn brings day, then night, again and again.
quests.funFact: Earth's steady turn is why we can plan our days with clocks and calendars.

quests.instruction: Where is it night when it is day in your home?
quests.correctAnswer: On the far side of Earth
options: On the surface of the Moon
On the far side of Earth
quests.hint: The Sun lights half of Earth.
quests.explanation: When it is day for us, it is night on the far side of Earth.
quests.funFact: It is night on the opposite side.

quests.instruction: Astronauts on the space station see many sunrises each day. Why?
quests.hint: They go around Earth about every 90 minutes.
quests.explanation: The station orbits Earth about every 90 minutes, so astronauts see about 16 sunrises a day.
quests.funFact: The International Space Station travels very fast.

quests.instruction: Why are some places having breakfast when others are having dinner?
quests.correctAnswer: Earth is turning, so times differ
options: Earth is turning, so times differ
Each country has its own Sun
quests.explanation: Because Earth is round and turning, different places are at different times of day.
quests.funFact: This is why we have time zones.

quests.instruction: Which best explains why we see stars at night?
quests.correctAnswer: Our side faces away from the Sun
options: The stars only switch on at night
Our side faces away from the Sun
quests.explanation: At night, the Sun's glare is gone, so stars are visible.
quests.funFact: Stars do not come on and off.

quests.instruction: Does the Moon cause night?
quests.correctAnswer: No, Earth turning away from the Sun does
options: No, Earth turning away from the Sun does
Yes, the Moon blocks the Sun every evening
quests.hint: Night happens even without a visible Moon.
quests.explanation: Night happens because Earth turns away from the Sun, even if the Moon is not visible.
quests.funFact: During a new Moon the Moon is nearly invisible, but night still happens.

quests.instruction: Which statement fits the Earth and Sun best?
quests.correctAnswer: Earth gets sunlight on one side at a time
options: Earth gets sunlight on one side at a time
Earth gets sunlight on all sides at once
quests.hint: A ball can only be lit from one direction.
quests.explanation: Sunlight reaches half the Earth at a time.
quests.funFact: That is why we have day and night.

quests.instruction: Mia holds a flashlight steady and slowly turns a ball in front of it. A small sticker on the ball moves from the lit side to the dark side. What does the sticker stand for?
quests.hint: Which way is the sticker moving: into the light, or out of it?
quests.explanation: A place that turns from the lit side into the dark side is going from day into night. That is what sunset looks like on Earth.
quests.funFact: Sunsets happen all over Earth, one place after another, as it spins.
